implementation_notes: NestJS makes the transporter configuration-only: register the client (ClientsModule.register([{ name: 'INVENTORY', transport: Transport.NATS }])), inject it by token and call client.send<Stock>({ cmd: 'check-stock' }, sku) for request-response - it returns an Observable with the response - or client.emit() for events; the server side declares @MessagePattern handlers. What replaces the classic gateway class is the injected client plus your own domain facade service, so application code names domain methods and the transport can be swapped without touching it.
pitfalls: ClientProxy is lazy: the connection is established before the first call, so the first request pays the connect cost unless connect() is called during bootstrap.
send() returns a request-response Observable - every subscription re-issues the request - so materialize it once (firstValueFrom/lastValueFrom) instead of passing it around like a promise.

Request-response needs two logical channels, which Nest compensates for on transports that lack them; for log-based streaming transporters the docs recommend the event style, so a gateway over Kafka is usually a design smell.

variants.name: Hand-written typed gateway over amqplib
variants.idiom_name: typed class over amqplib publish/consume with correlationId
variants.implementation_notes: Without the framework the gateway is a typed class over amqplib: methods publish with channel.publish and await a Promise resolved from the reply consumer that matches correlationId; the promise map, the reply queue and the timeout are hand-written, while amqplib contributes the protocol handling only. Choose this when the service must not depend on a framework (libraries, lambdas, CLIs) but a plain broker client is acceptable.
pitfalls: channel.publish returns a boolean, not a promise: handle 'false' as backpressure ('drain'), otherwise messages are silently held in memory.
A channel that encountered an error is invalid for good, so the gateway must be able to rebuild channels instead of caching them in a field.
Promises in the pending map must reject on timeout; a promise that is never settled keeps the awaiting request alive forever.
